item.title: Modern Hardware
item.description: The main disadvantage of the supercomputers of the 1960s wasn’t that they were slow — relatively speaking, they weren’t — but that they were giant, complex to use, and so expensive that only the governments of the world superpowers could afford them. Their size was the reason they were so expensive: they required a lot of custom components that had to be very carefully assembled in the macro-world, by people holding advanced degrees in electrical engineering, in a process that couldn’t be scaled up for mass production.

item.title: Programming Languages
item.description: If you are reading this book, then somewhere on your computer science journey you had a moment when you first started to care about the efficiency of your code. Mine was in high school, when I realized that making websites and doing useful programming won’t get you into a university, and entered the exciting world of algorithmic programming olympiads. I was an okay programmer, especially for a highschooler, but I had never really wondered how much time it took for my code to execute before.

item.title: Models of Computation
item.description: Consider two procedures that both read every element of an array exactly once. The first reads the elements from left to right. The second follows a permutation stored in the array and uses the value it has just read to find the next element. In the usual operation-counting model, these procedures are almost identical: both perform $n$ reads and $O(n)$ integer operations. On an actual computer, they can behave very differently.

item.title: When to Optimize
item.description: Suppose a request spends most of its time waiting for a database. Replacing an integer division in the response formatter with a shift may produce magnificent assembly and an entirely invisible product improvement. Performance engineering begins one step before optimization: deciding what is worth making faster. #Choose the Objective“Fast” is not a complete requirement. Depending on the application, the quantity we care about may be: latency: how long one operation takes; throughput: how many operations finish per unit of time; tail latency: how long an unusually slow operation takes; resource efficiency: CPU time, memory, energy, or money per operation; scalability: how performance changes with input size or load.
